Early HFNC Flow Intensity and Subsequent Invasive Mechanical Ventilation

Abstract

View Published Abstract

Background

High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is commonly used for acute respiratory failure (ARF) in critically ill adults, but whether higher HFNC flow intensity primarily reflects underlying illness severity or identifies patients at increased risk of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) remains unclear. We therefore investigated whether maximum HFNC flow during the first 24 hours after initiation was associated with subsequent IMV after adjustment for comorbidity burden and illness severity.

Methods

We conducted a cohort study using electronic health record data from Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital in the UCSF De-Identified Clinical Data Warehouse. De-identified data are available to UCSF researchers after a data use agreement; IRB approval was not required. Adults (≥18 y) admitted to an ICU from 2019–2025 who received HFNC at ≥30 L/min were included. Patients were excluded if they received IMV before HFNC initiation or had do-not-resuscitate orders at HFNC initiation.

The exposure was the maximum HFNC flow during the first 24 hours after HFNC initiation. A 24-hour landmark design was used to minimize immortal time bias; follow-up began 24 hours after HFNC initiation and continued through 28 days. Patients who died or were intubated within the first 24 hours were excluded.

Covariates included the Elixhauser comorbidity index, SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio, respiratory rate, and vasopressor use during initial HFNC therapy. Time to IMV was analyzed using Fine–Gray subdistribution hazards models with death treated as a competing event. Adjusted cumulative incidence of IMV was estimated across common HFNC flow rates (30, 40, 50, and 60 L/min).

Results

After data cleaning, 233 unique cases were analyzed. Higher maximum HFNC flow was independently associated with a greater hazard of IMV after adjusting for comorbidity burden and illness severity. Every 10 L/min increase in flow was associated with a 38% increase in the subdistribution hazard of IMV (sHR 1.38, 95% CI 1.07–1.77; p=0.012). Respiratory rate was also independently associated with IMV, with every 5-breath/min increase associated with a 33% increase in the subdistribution hazard (sHR 1.33, 95% CI 1.16–1.53; p<0.001). Elixhauser comorbidity index, SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio, and vasopressor use were not statistically significant after adjustment.

Conclusion

Among critically ill adults receiving HFNC, higher HFNC flow intensity during the first 24 hours was associated with increased hazard of IMV after accounting for comorbidity burden and illness severity.

Study Design

Data Source

Cohort Construction

This cohort study used de-identified electronic health record data from Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital available through the UCSF De-Identified Clinical Data Warehouse (DeID-CDW). The DeID-CDW provides UCSF researchers access to de-identified clinical data for research purposes.

SFDPH data available in DeID-CDW: >1.2 million patients as of December 2024.
Learn more about SFDPH/ZSFG data in the DeID-CDW

The eligible study population was defined using prespecified eligibility criteria.

After application of the 24-hour landmark, 236 patients remained eligible. Three patients were excluded from the complete-case analysis because S/F ratio data were unavailable, resulting in a final analytic cohort of 233 patients.

Eligibility

Inclusion

  • Adults ≥18 years
  • Admitted to an ICU
  • HFNC ≥30 L/min

Exclusion

  • IMV before HFNC initiation
  • DNR order at HFNC initiation
  • Death or intubation within the first 24 hours

Landmark Design

24-Hour Landmark

Maximum HFNC flow was defined using measurements during the first 24 hours after HFNC initiation. Because this exposure cannot be fully determined until the 24-hour window has elapsed, beginning outcome follow-up at HFNC initiation could introduce immortal time bias.

A 24-hour landmark design was therefore used to align exposure ascertainment with the start of follow-up. Patients who died or were intubated during the first 24 hours were excluded. Follow-up for subsequent IMV began at the 24-hour landmark (T₀) and continued through day 28.

Conceptual Model

View directed acyclic graph (DAG)

Maximum HFNC flow during the first 24 hours was the exposure and subsequent IMV was the outcome. Measured covariates included the van Walraven–weighted Elixhauser score, respiratory rate, S/F ratio, and vasopressor use.

Residual confounding from evolving illness severity and clinical decision-making may remain.

Primary Analysis

Outcome

The primary outcome was time from the 24-hour landmark (T₀) to first invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) through day 28.

Fine–Gray Competing-Risk Model

The primary analysis used Fine–Gray subdistribution hazards regression to estimate the association between maximum HFNC flow during the first 24 hours and the cumulative incidence of subsequent IMV.

Death prior to IMV was treated as a competing event.

The model was adjusted for:

  • Elixhauser comorbidity index
  • SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio
  • Respiratory rate
  • Vasopressor use during initial HFNC therapy
Why a competing-risk model?

Death precludes subsequent intubation and therefore represents a competing event rather than a simple censoring event.

Treating death as a competing event allows estimation of the cumulative incidence of IMV while accounting for competing mortality.

Adjusted Cumulative Incidence of IMV

Adjusted cumulative incidence was estimated across maximum HFNC flow rates of 30, 40, 50, and 60 L/min.

Sensitivity Analysis

Cause-Specific Cox Model

A cause-specific Cox proportional hazards model was performed as a sensitivity analysis.

In this model:

  • IMV was treated as the event of interest.
  • Death prior to IMV was treated as a censoring event.
  • Discharge and administrative end of follow-up were treated as censoring events.

The cause-specific model estimates the instantaneous hazard of IMV among patients who remain alive and not yet intubated.

The association between maximum HFNC flow and subsequent IMV was similar in the cause-specific analysis:

HR 1.43 per 10 L/min increase (95% CI 1.09–1.87, p = 0.010).

Interpretation

Higher maximum HFNC flow during the first 24 hours remained associated with subsequent IMV after adjustment for measured comorbidity burden and illness severity.

Respiratory rate was also associated with subsequent IMV, while Elixhauser comorbidity index, SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio, and vasopressor use were not statistically significant after adjustment.

HFNC flow is clinician-titrated and may reflect both evolving respiratory support needs and clinical decision-making. The observed association may therefore reflect residual severity not captured by the available covariates and should not be interpreted as evidence that higher HFNC flow causes intubation.

The consistency of the Fine–Gray and cause-specific Cox estimates supports the robustness of the observed association across the two modeling approaches.

Conclusion

Among critically ill adults receiving HFNC, higher maximum HFNC flow during the first 24 hours of therapy was associated with subsequent IMV after adjustment for measured comorbidity burden and illness severity.

Limitations

Considerations for Interpretation

  • Residual confounding: Comprehensive severity scores (e.g., SOFA, APACHE) and respiratory failure etiology were not included; available EHR measures may incompletely capture evolving illness severity.

  • Confounding by indication and practice variation: HFNC flow is clinician-selected and may be increased in response to worsening respiratory failure, while thresholds for subsequent intubation may vary across providers.

  • Generalizability: Single-center ICU cohort; findings may not extend to patients receiving HFNC outside the ICU or at other institutions.

  • EHR-derived data: Cohort definitions, exposures, outcomes, and covariates depend on the completeness and accuracy of routinely collected clinical data.

Supplementary Methods

Variable Definitions

Key study variables and derived measures are defined below.

Key Variable Definitions
Variable Definition
Maximum HFNC flow Maximum HFNC flow recorded during the first 24 hours after HFNC initiation.
24-hour landmark (T₀) Timepoint 24 hours after HFNC initiation. Patients who died or were intubated before T₀ were excluded.
Invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) First invasive mechanical ventilation occurring after the 24-hour landmark and through day 28.
S/F ratio SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio used for adjustment in the primary model.
Respiratory rate Respiratory rate used for adjustment in the primary model.
Elixhauser comorbidity score Encounter-level comorbidities were identified from ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes using the Quan Elixhauser mapping and weighted using the van Walraven point system. Condition-specific weights were summed to produce an overall score, with higher scores indicating greater weighted comorbidity burden. The encounter primary diagnosis was retained separately from the Elixhauser calculation.
Vasopressor use Vasoactive medication exposure overlapping any portion of the first 24 hours after HFNC initiation.
Death Death before IMV during follow-up, treated as a competing event in the primary Fine–Gray analysis.

Missing Data

The 24-hour landmark cohort included 236 patients. Three patients (1.3%) had missing S/F ratio data and were excluded from complete-case adjusted analyses, resulting in an analytic cohort of 233 patients.

Statistical Software

Analyses were performed using R version 4.4.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
